To indemnify someone means to protect them from financial loss — either by preventing them from bearing that loss in the first place, or by paying them back after the loss has already happened.

Think of it as a promise that says: "If something goes wrong and you lose money (or get sued, or suffer damages), I will make sure you don't end up worse off because of it."

The word works in two directions — one looking forward, one looking backward.

1. Protection before a loss happens (forward-looking)
This is a promise made in advance. One party tells another: "Don't worry — if you suffer a loss because of this deal or this situation, I will cover it." The loss hasn't happened yet, but you are already shielded from it because someone has committed to absorbing it on your behalf.

2. Compensation after a loss happens (backward-looking)
This is the fulfillment of that promise. The loss has now occurred, and the party who promised to protect you steps in and pays — covering your damages, expenses, or liability. You are "made whole," meaning you are restored to the financial position you were in before things went wrong.

In practice, indemnifying someone usually involves both: first the promise, then the payout when needed.

Imagine you are a delivery driver hired by a company. While making a delivery, you accidentally damage someone's car. The injured person sues you.

If your employer has agreed to indemnify you, it means:

  • They will step in and handle the legal costs.
  • They will pay any damages awarded against you.
  • You personally will not have to pay out of your own pocket.

The employer has taken the financial burden off your shoulders and placed it on their own. That is indemnification in action.
The Most Common Real-World Context: Contracts

Indemnify appears most often in contracts and legal agreements. Almost every professional contract — employment agreements, business deals, service contracts — contains what is called an indemnification clause (or "indemnity clause").

This clause spells out exactly who indemnifies whom, and for what kinds of losses. For example:

  • A software company might indemnify its clients against lawsuits claiming the software violates someone else's copyright.
  • A contractor might be required to indemnify the building owner against injuries that occur on the job site.
  • An employer often indemnifies employees for actions they take while doing their job — so an employee is not personally ruined if something goes wrong during the normal course of work.

The party doing the protecting is called the indemnitor. The party being protected is called the indemnitee.
Insurance: The Most Familiar Form of Indemnification

Insurance is essentially indemnification on a mass scale. When you buy an insurance policy:

  • You pay a premium.
  • The insurance company indemnifies you — meaning they promise that if a covered loss occurs (your car is wrecked, your house burns, you fall ill), they will pay for it.
  • You do not end up in a worse financial position than you were before the disaster.

This is why the goal of most insurance payouts is to restore, not enrich — to bring you back to where you were, no more, no less. That principle is called the principle of indemnity, and it sits at the very heart of what indemnify means.
A Crucial Distinction: Indemnify vs. Simply "Pay"

You might wonder: isn't indemnifying someone just... paying them? Not quite. The word carries specific weight:

  • When you pay someone, it could be for anything — a service, a product, a gift.
  • When you indemnify someone, you are specifically covering a loss, liability, or harm — something they should not have to bear themselves. The payment is corrective or protective in nature.

The word implies a responsibility being transferred from one party to another. The indemnitee (the protected person) is not supposed to suffer — and the indemnitor (the protecting party) has taken on the obligation to make sure they don't.

Not all indemnification is unlimited. In contracts, the scope is usually defined carefully:

  • Full indemnification: The protecting party covers all losses, no matter what.
  • Limited indemnification: The protecting party covers only certain types of losses (e.g., only third-party claims, not the other party's own negligence).
  • Capped indemnification: The protection only goes up to a certain dollar amount.

Courts also generally will not enforce an indemnification clause that protects someone from the consequences of their own gross negligence or intentional wrongdoing. The law draws a line there.

• Indemnification (noun): The act or process of indemnifying; also the actual compensation paid. "The contract required indemnification for all third-party claims."
  • Indemnity (noun): The protection itself, or the sum of money paid as compensation. "He received indemnity for the losses caused by the flood." You may also see phrases like "letter of indemnity" or "indemnity insurance."
  • Indemnified (past tense/past participle): "She was fully indemnified by her employer."

To indemnify someone is to formally take responsibility for protecting them from financial loss — either by promising in advance to cover any damages that arise, or by actually compensating them after a loss has occurred, so that they are left no worse off than before.
